Dear Dr. Bradley,

I would appreciate your evaluation of Mr. Colin Myers, a 44-year-old gentleman who was recently admitted to our medical service. His history of exertional intolerance extends back to his childhood, with the initial episodes of severe muscle aches and diffuse soreness noted around age seven.

He presented acutely earlier this week following a moderate workout, reporting intense muscular pain. Laboratory evaluation confirmed a massive acute breakdown of skeletal muscle, with serum creatine kinase levels climbing above 40,000 U/L. Concurrent with this, he passed dark, tea-colored urine that tested strongly positive for filtered heme pigments in the absence of red blood cells. The event was further complicated by impaired kidney function, with his serum creatinine doubling from his documented baseline. 

On physical examination, he demonstrates strikingly enlarged and bulky musculature throughout both calves and thighs. In contrast, the muscle bulk across his upper limbs is completely unremarkable, with no signs of enlargement in the arms or shoulders. Deep tendon reflexes are preserved, sensation is intact, and cranial nerve testing is fully normal. He works as an accountant, does not smoke, drinks alcohol only on rare social occasions, and takes no regular medications. There is no family history of neuromuscular disorders.

Given his long-standing history of exercise-triggered muscle necrosis and secondary renal impairment, I would be grateful for your expert assessment and guidance on how best to evaluate him further.

Sincerely,

Dr. Julian Howard
